lead: Some circuits have many storage elements, and solving each differential equation separately gets messy. State-variable analysis collects the inductor currents and capacitor voltages into one vector x. The circuit then becomes two matrix equations, ẋ = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du. The eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies, so you know whether the circuit rings without solving anything. Only a few universities teach this chapter. Circuit simulators and control engineers use it daily.
prereq: You need: second-order RLC circuits for the characteristic equation, network functions for poles, and basic matrix algebra.

blocks.text: State variables are the quantities that cannot jump when a switch moves: inductor currents iL and capacitor voltages vC (see initial and final conditions). Stack them as x₁, x₂, … into the state vector x. Usually there is one state per storage element; a loop made only of capacitors (and voltage sources), or a cut-set made only of inductors (and current sources), makes one of them dependent and lowers the count.

blocks.where: x is the n × 1 state vector; u holds the m source values; A is n × n and B is n × m.
y holds the p chosen outputs; C is p × n. D is p × m and carries the direct path from the sources to the outputs: it is nonzero only when an output depends on a source at the same instant.

items: Label each independent i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub> as a state.
Write KVL round a loop containing each inductor and KCL at a node of each capacitor.
Rearrange until each derivative stands alone, with only states and sources on the right.
Collect the coefficients into A and B.
Write each output in terms of states and sources to read C and D.

blocks.where: I is the identity matrix of the same size as A.

blocks.text: For a series RLC this is the characteristic polynomial s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) of second-order RLC circuits, so the eigenvalues show whether the circuit rings without solving any differential equation. Real negative roots decay; a pair −σ ± jω_d rings at ωd while decaying; a passive RLC never gives a positive real part. For a 2 × 2 A, match det(sI − A) with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² to read ωn and ζ.

Figure 5.9.1 marks the two states on the worked example's circuit. The source enters only the inductor equation, through B; the two states feed each other through A; and the output picks out v<sub>C</sub> through C. Each state is the integral of its derivative, which is why x cannot jump. With a DC input the final state follows from ẋ = 0, that is Ax(∞) + Bu = 0, without solving anything else.

figure.caption: The worked example: the inductor current x₁ and the capacitor voltage x₂ are the two states of the series RLC. Its state matrices give det(sI − A) = s² + 4s + 20, whose roots −2 ± j4 are the natural frequencies.

spec.aria: A series circuit of source v s, 2 ohms, 0.5 henry and 0.1 farad with the inductor current marked x1 and the capacitor voltage marked x2, beside the matrices A equal to minus 4, minus 2; 10, 0 and B equal to 2; 0, C equal to 0, 1, D equal to 0, and the roots minus 2 plus or minus j4.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has R = 2 Ω, L = 0.5 H and C = 0.1 F, driven by v<sub>s</sub>(t). Take x₁ = i<sub>L</sub> and x₂ = v<sub>C</sub>, and the output y = v<sub>C</sub>. Find A, B, C and D, the natural frequencies, and the final state for a 10 V DC input.
steps: KVL round the loop: v<sub>s</sub> = 2i<sub>L</sub> + 0.5 di<sub>L</sub>/dt + v<sub>C</sub>, so di<sub>L</sub>/dt = −4i<sub>L</sub> − 2v<sub>C</sub> + 2v<sub>s</sub>.
KCL at the capacitor: 0.1 dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = i<sub>L</sub>, so dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = 10i<sub>L</sub>.
Matrix form, writing rows separated by a semicolon: A = [−4, −2; 10, 0] and B = [2; 0].
Output y = v<sub>C</sub> = 0·i<sub>L</sub> + 1·v<sub>C</sub> + 0·v<sub>s</sub>, so C = [0, 1] and D = [0].
det(sI − A) = (s + 4)s + 20 = s² + 4s + 20. Check: R/L = 4 and 1/(LC) = 20, the series RLC polynomial. ✓

Final state for v<sub>s</sub> = 10 V: set ẋ = 0. The second row gives 10i<sub>L</sub> = 0, so i<sub>L</sub>(∞) = 0; the first gives −2v<sub>C</sub> + 20 = 0, so v<sub>C</sub>(∞) = 10 V, as the open capacitor predicts.
examples.answer: A = [−4, −2; 10, 0], B = [2; 0], C = [0, 1], D = [0]; natural frequencies −2 ± j4 s⁻¹ (ω<sub>n</sub> = 4.47 rad/s, ζ = 0.447); final state i<sub>L</sub> = 0, v<sub>C</sub> = 10 V.
examples.check:
import numpy as np
A=np.array([[-4,-2],[10,0]]);B=np.array([2,0])
print(np.linalg.eigvals(A), np.linalg.solve(A,-B*10))

traps: Making a resistor voltage or a capacitor current a state. Only i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub> store energy and stay continuous.
Sign slips in A: in the series RLC the i<sub>L</sub> row has −R/L on the diagonal and −1/L against v<sub>C</sub>.
Writing 1 instead of 1/L in B. A voltage source enters the inductor equation divided by L.

Guessing D. Read it from the output equation: v<sub>C</sub> = x₂ gives D = 0, but the inductor voltage v<sub>L</sub> = v<sub>s</sub> − Ri<sub>L</sub> − v<sub>C</sub> depends on the source directly, so D = 1.

quiz.q: Which quantities are the state variables of an RLC circuit?
quiz.a: The inductor currents and the capacitor voltages (the independent ones).

quiz.q: Why can a resistor voltage not be a state variable?
quiz.a: A resistor stores no energy and its voltage can jump at switching, so it does not carry the circuit's memory; it can always be written from the states and sources.

quiz.q: Series RL: R = 2 Ω, L = 0.5 H, state x = i, input v<sub>s</sub>. Find A and B.
quiz.a: v<sub>s</sub> = 2i + 0.5 di/dt, so di/dt = −4i + 2v<sub>s</sub>: A = [−4], B = [2].

quiz.q: For the worked example, take the output as the inductor voltage v<sub>L</sub> instead. Write C and D.
quiz.a: v<sub>L</sub> = v<sub>s</sub> − 2i<sub>L</sub> − v<sub>C</sub>, so C = [−2, −1] and D = [1].

quiz.q: A = [0, 1; −2, −3]. Find the natural frequencies and say how the circuit responds.
quiz.a: det(sI − A) = s² + 3s + 2 = (s + 1)(s + 2), so s = −1 and −2 s⁻¹: two real negative roots, an overdamped response with no ringing.

quiz.q: The eigenvalues of A are −0.5 ± j3 s⁻¹. Describe the response.
quiz.a: A decaying oscillation: a sinusoid at 3 rad/s inside the envelope e<sup>−0.5t</sup>, which falls by about 99 % in 5/0.5 = 10 s.

beyond: Not for the exam. State-space matrices A, B, C, D are the standard language of control engineering; search state-space representation and controllability and observability. Circuit simulators assemble the same matrices internally, which is why SPICE handles thousands of nodes. Power-electronics engineers average the equations over a switching cycle, called state-space averaging. A later course solves ẋ = Ax + Bu with the state-transition matrix eAt.
